Hiring: IAM Engineer – Java/Python Engineer
Location: Glasgow, UK
Work Mode: Hybrid – 3 Days in Office per Week
Employment Type: Contract
Experience Required: 8+ Years
Job Description
We are looking for an experienced IAM Engineer – Java/Python Engineer with 8+ years of experience in Java development, Python scripting, Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Directory Services. The ideal candidate will have hands-on experience with enterprise Java applications, Python automation, Linux/RHEL environments, and directory services platforms such as PingDS (ForgeRock DS).
The role involves supporting IAM platforms, developing and maintaining Java-based components, automating migration and deployment activities, troubleshooting production issues, and improving operational efficiency through scripting and modern engineering practices.
Key Responsibilities and Required Skills
Strong hands-on experience in Java development, including troubleshooting, debugging, code enhancements, API development, integration development, and enterprise Java applications.
Hands-on experience in Python development for automation, utilities, APIs, integrations, data processing, and production-quality scripting.
Experience supporting IAM and Directory Services platforms, preferably PingDS (ForgeRock DS), including migration, upgrades, configuration, deployment, and production support.
Experience with PingDS plugins, extensions, custom integrations, and Java-based directory services components is highly desirable.
Strong knowledge of Linux/RHEL, including filesystem management, permissions, processes, services, networking, log analysis, and performance troubleshooting.
Proficiency in Bash/Shell scripting and Python automation for migration, deployment, validation, reconciliation, monitoring, and operational activities.
Familiarity with LDAP/LDAPS, directory services, replication, schemas, certificates, TLS, REST APIs, JSON, and IAM security fundamentals.
Experience with Git, CI/CD pipelines, Maven/Gradle, Python package management, testing frameworks, code reviews, and secure coding practices.
Basic understanding of AI/GenAI concepts and practical experience using AI-assisted coding tools such as GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, or equivalent for code generation, refactoring, scripting, testing, documentation, and troubleshooting.
Ability to validate AI-generated code and follow secure development and responsible AI usage practices.
Knowledge of C/C++ will be an added advantage.

🚨 HIRING — COUNTERPART HEALTH

📌 Position: Data Analyst, Clinical Data Effectiveness
📍 Location: Remote (Anywhere in the World)
📄 Contract type: Full-Time

JOB DESCRIPTION
Counterpart Health is an AI-powered physician enablement platform that delivers clinical insights to providers at the point of care. As a Data Analyst, you will serve as the Subject Matter Expert (SME) for clinical data completeness and effectiveness, owning the end-to-end understanding of our clinical data lifecycle.

KEY RESPONSIBILITIES
• Proactively identify and monitor healthcare facilities that generate high-quality clinical documents to quantify data gaps.
• Conduct deep-dive analyses by mapping and correlating facility-specific data across disparate sources like structured claims, clinical care summaries (CCDAs), and ADT messages.
• Establish and maintain reporting on ADT coverage across key geographic, organizational, and technological dimensions.
• Recommend and guide the implementation of optimal technical configurations for existing data vendors.
• Conduct evaluations and proof-of-concepts for potential new data integration technologies.
• Systematically determine the existence and completeness of documentation associated with specific patient visits.
• Develop a data-driven framework for prioritizing facility targets for direct data acquisition.
• Inform and guide vendor strategy around national initiatives such as TEFCA and QHIN adoption.
• Partner cross-functionally with Product Managers, Engineers, and Clinical teams.

REQUIREMENTS
• Experience with TEFCA/QHIN frameworks and evolving national interoperability standards.
• Familiarity with vendor-specific data exchange platforms (e.g., Bamboo Health, HSX, Particle Health, Kno2).
• Background in value-based care, population health, or clinical data operations.
• Experience with claims-clinical data reconciliation.
• Comfort working with Python or similar tools for data manipulation and automation.

Something’s shifted in what GCs are asking us for this year, and it’s not more lawyers. 

It’s legal ops people. Loads of them. 

Demand for legal operations roles at SJP has gone through the roof - contract managers, legal tech leads, people who can sort out a matter management system that nobody’s touched since 2019. A couple of years ago these were the odd request. Now they’re some of the first calls we get. 

I think it makes sense when you look at what’s actually going on. Teams are under pressure to do more without adding headcount, AI tools are landing faster than anyone can work out how to use them, and finance wants data on where legal spend is going. None of that gets fixed by hiring another senior associate. 

It gets fixed by someone who knows how the work flows. Who can look at a team and say “this bit should be automated, this bit should be a playbook, and this bit genuinely needs a lawyer.” 

Funny thing is, plenty of legal teams still treat ops as a nice-to-have. Something to sort out once things calm down. 

Things don’t calm down. The teams getting this right are the ones who’ve realised ops isn’t overhead. It’s what makes everyone else’s time worth more. 

If you’re a GC wondering whether a legal ops hire (or a few months of interim support) could free your lawyers up, drop me a message. Happy to chat it through, no pitch. And if you’re in legal ops and open to new projects, we’d love to hear from you too.

I just got a DM telling me I hadn't wasted my law degree.

The first problem here is that I didn't go to law school. The second one (the bigger issue) is that the DM demonstrates exactly the iceberg we're all sailing towards. We're losing the ability to learn good judgement.

A couple of weeks ago I gave a talk at the OPI European Forum event: Who's checking the work? Trust, judgement and the future of work.

My entire thesis is that companies are moving to a future where much of the repetitive and so-called 'mundane' work is being done by AI. That new entrants into the world of work will need to become skilled validators of AI output - but (and it's a very big BUT), in a few years there will be no one left for them to learn those skills from. 

I used the legal profession as an example of how this is already happening. Graduates who used to spend hours reading contracts and reports now pass on the output of AI to their seniors. 

One senior lawyer I spoke to in the European Commission told me that, where he once spent 20 minutes reviewing work from graduates, he's now spending hours checking their work. 

This is key: Human mistakes follow patterns a senior has learned to spot, and AI mistakes don’t, so checking takes longer.

All of which came to mind when I read the DM.

We are now hiring validators.

I am working with leaders to help them understand what they need to do now to ensure their new employees learn the skills that keep trust and judgement in their companies.

🚨 Cybersecurity has a talent shortage? Or does it have an employer problem?

Companies constantly complain about the shortage of qualified cybersecurity professionals. Yet, when I look at job listings, I see an increasing number of six month contracts, daily rate positions, and roles demanding years of experience with little employment security.

You want experienced professionals to protect your infrastructure, prevent data breaches, and manage critical security risks, but offering them job security is apparently too much to ask?

Let’s be clear: cybersecurity isn’t a six-month problem.

With AI accelerating the evolution of cyber threats, organisations need skilled professionals more than ever. Building effective security teams requires continuity, investment, and institutional knowledge.

I’m not against contracting. But flexibility for employers shouldn’t automatically mean insecurity for workers.

And let’s address another contradiction:

How can companies complain about a skills shortage while refusing to invest in junior talent and demanding senior level experience for almost every position?

As a cybersecurity professional, I want fair compensation, career progression and the opportunity to grow within an organisation, not the constant uncertainty of finding another job every six months.

Maybe the real problem isn’t that companies can’t find cybersecurity talent. Maybe it’s that cybersecurity talent can’t find companies worth committing to.

Recruiters and hiring managers: If cybersecurity is so critical to your business, why aren’t you investing in the long term careers of the people protecting it?

3 enterprise deals stalled this quarter on the same question: "Show us your AI authorization policy."

They mean something specific - a document that says: here are the decisions our AI makes autonomously, and here is where a human reviews or overrides. Different from SOC 2, different from a system architecture diagram.

Most founders don't have it written down. Many encounter the question mid-deal.

EU AI Act Article 13 is going to formalize this for many AI systems. Enterprise procurement teams are already 12-18 months ahead of enforcement on this.

Three well-built products this year - genuine results, happy pilot users - stalled at the contract stage on one document that probably takes two hours to draft.

If your AI makes consequential decisions - financial, operational, hiring, clinical - does your authorization policy exist on paper?
